On this page

  • Bach: “O Haupt voll Blut und Wunden” (“O Sacred Head, Now Wounded”)
  • Beethoven: Piano Sonata No. 14 in C♯ minor (“Moonlight”), I

Analysed Scores

Two real pieces with expert Roman-numeral analyses under the notes, from the When in Rome corpus: Bach’s chorale “O Haupt voll Blut und Wunden” (“O Sacred Head, Now Wounded”) and the first movement of Beethoven’s “Moonlight” Sonata, each with two analysts’ readings to compare. Play along with the analysis.

Real music, analysed by experts, with the Roman numerals under the notes where each chord begins. Each piece has two analyses by different analysts, in tabs: compare them. They often agree, and where they don’t, both readings can be defended. The analyses come from When in Rome, a collection of harmonic analyses gathered by Mark Gotham and others.

Reading the labels: a key followed by a colon (d:) means the music has moved to that key (capital letter major, small letter minor); the numerals after it are in the new key. The figures are those of Chapter 16 (6, 64, 7, 65, 43, 42). ° is diminished and ø half-diminished, as in the book. V/iv and vii°7/V are the secondary chords of Chapters 17 and 18; N6 is the Neapolitan. A numeral sits under the bass where its chord starts; where the bass holds a note through a chord change, the note is written as tied notes so the label has a place (it sounds the same). Resizing: drag the line at the right edge of a score to make it wider or narrower (double-click it to reset); the bars re-flow to fit, and the size is kept for every score on the page.

Bach: “O Haupt voll Blut und Wunden” (“O Sacred Head, Now Wounded”)

From the St Matthew Passion (BWV 244.54; no. 74 in Riemenschneider’s collection of the chorales). Bach harmonized this melody several times; this is one of them. Listen for the key changes: the phrases end in F, then D minor, then B♭ and G minor, then C and back to F. Each new key is reached through its own dominant, as in Chapter 22. The two analysts mostly agree. Where they differ, look at bars 6 and 7. In bar 6, one analyst reads IV64 where the other reads a cadential 6/4. In bar 7, one reads Imaj7 where the other reads I7.

  • Dmitri Tymoczko
  • Bach Chorales Melody-Harmony Corpus

Analysis: Dmitri Tymoczko.

The analyst’s notes:

  • please email corrections to dmitri@princeton.edu
  • unusual vi-viio-I progression where leading tone falls in soprano; could read first two chords as i-iv in d.
  • quarter-note suspension in tenor, beat 3
  • the first beat of m7 can be read either as a deceptive cadence to vi6 or as Imaj7 followed by a lower neighbor, or as a combination of these.

Other readings the analyst gives:

  • Bar 1: IV viiø⁴₃ I⁶ ii vii°⁶ I
  • Bar 7: vi⁶ g: i⁶ V⁶₅ i
  • Bar 7: IM⁷ g: i⁶ V⁶₅ i

Analysis: Bach Chorales Melody-Harmony Corpus (BCMH).

Beethoven: Piano Sonata No. 14 in C♯ minor (“Moonlight”), I

The whole first movement (Adagio sostenuto). Triplets run under a slow melody throughout. The harmony changes slowly, usually once or twice a bar, so this is a good piece for following an analysis by ear. Things to find:

  • the Neapolitan (N6) in bar 3 and again later;
  • the move to E major (the relative major) in bars 7–9;
  • the long stretch of dominant harmony (V7 and i64 taking turns, bars 28–41) before the return;
  • the sections the first analysis marks: exposition, development, recapitulation, coda.
  • Tsung-Ping Chen and Li Su
  • Dmitri Tymoczko

Analysis: Tsung-Ping Chen and Li Su (BPS dataset), proof-read by Mark Gotham.

Analysis: Dmitri Tymoczko.

The analyst’s notes:

  • chords here are pretty hard to identify, though the general gist is clear; either VI or Ger or viio7/V
  • the point of key shift here is very elusive as is the nature of the f#64 passing chord (iv64? i64 still in f#?)
  • “flat five” dominant ninth (D7/G# in C# minor) on beat 2

Other readings the analyst gives:

  • Bar 16: VIM⁷ vii°⁷/V
  • Bar 16: Ger⁴₃
  • Bar 25: i c♯: iv vii°⁶₅ iv⁶₄
For teachers
  • Sources: the analyses are When in Rome’s RomanText files, CC BY-SA 4.0, shown as they are (signs written as in the book: ° ø, figures run together). The scores are Craig Sapp’s Humdrum encodings of public-domain editions, converted to ABC by scripts/when-in-rome/build.mjs. That script also places each numeral at its bar and beat, and the browser test checks every converted note against the original encoding.
  • Notes and other readings: where an analyst left notes or alternative readings in the file, they are listed under the score.
  • Not edited: the analyses are not this site’s, and some labels follow the analyst’s conventions rather than the book’s (Cad64, Imaj7, I7).
  • More pieces: the corpus has hundreds more (all the Bach chorales, Beethoven’s sonatas and quartets, 19th-century songs). The same script can add them.

Chen, Tsung-Ping, and Li Su. BPS-FH: Beethoven Piano Sonata with Functional Harmony dataset (ISMIR 2018). GitHub. github.com/Tsung-Ping/functional-harmony. The source of the first Moonlight analysis, converted to RomanText and proof-read by Mark Gotham for When in Rome.

Gotham, Mark, et al. When in Rome: A Meta-Corpus of Functional Harmony. GitHub. github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome. The analyses on this page (RomanText files), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Nápoles López, Néstor, et al. BCMH: The Bach Chorales Melody-Harmony Corpus. GitHub. github.com/napulen/BCMH. The second chorale analysis (automated translation to RomanText).

Sapp, Craig Stuart, encoder. 370 Four-part Chorales by J. S. Bach in the Humdrum File Format. GitHub. github.com/craigsapp/bach-370-chorales. The chorale’s notes (after Dörffel’s edition, Breitkopf & Härtel, c. 1875), converted to ABC for this page.

Sapp, Craig Stuart, encoder. Beethoven Piano Sonatas in the Humdrum File Format (after the Durand 1915 edition, ed. Paul Dukas). GitHub. github.com/craigsapp/beethoven-piano-sonatas. The sonata’s notes, converted to ABC for this page.

Tymoczko, Dmitri, analyst. Roman-numeral analyses of the Bach chorales and of Beethoven, Piano Sonata Op. 27 No. 2, in When in Rome. github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome/tree/master/Corpus.
